think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: The patient presents with a solitary, massive (20 cm) cutaneous plaque featuring lichenification and ulcerated margins, mimicking non-infectious inflammatory dermatoses (psoriasis, lichen simplex) or deep endemic mycoses.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The presentation ends after clinical history and physical description of the cutaneous lesion. Montenegro skin testing, indirect immunofluorescence, lesion smear cytology, and culture represent confirmatory investigations.
3. Differential Distinctions: Lichen simplex and psoriasis lack ulceration and intracellular parasites; chromomycosis and paracoccidioidomycosis exhibit characteristic fungal spores or muriform cells. Cutaneous leishmaniasis is confirmed by demonstrating amastigotes on lesion scrapings and positive Montenegro skin test.
case_prompt: A 45-year-old male residing in Apucarana, Paraná, Brazil, presented for evaluation of an atypical cutaneous lesion on the right side of his back that had been present for approximately one month. Before presentation, the patient had applied topical antibiotic ointments without clinical improvement. On physical examination, there was a solitary rounded plaque measuring 20 cm in diameter, characterized by an erythematous-violaceous center, desquamative and ulcerated edges, and a broad surrounding area of prominent lichenification.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The prominent plaque architecture, desquamation, and marked lichenification clinically mimicked chronic inflammatory or papulosquamous dermatoses, but ulcerated margins, refractoriness to conservative topical measures, and parasite demonstration excluded them.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Based on clinical appearance, the differential diagnosis of the lesion included chronic simple lichen, psoriasis, squamous cell carcinoma, chromomycosis, cutaneous tuberculosis, syphilis, paracoccidioidomycosis, and sarcoidosis.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Endemic South American subcutaneous fungal infections frequently manifest as large, verrucous, or ulcerated plaques, but mycological examinations were negative.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: To exclude the possibility of coexisting infections, fungi and HIV investigations were performed with negative results.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Direct examination of lesion scrapings stained with Giemsa identified Leishmania amastigotes, supported by culture in blood base agar, a positive Montenegro skin test (10 mm induration), and positive indirect immunofluorescence.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Leishmania amastigotes were detected in the material obtained by scraping of the lesion stained by Giemsa (Fig. 1B) and cultured in blood base agar (BBA).
